transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-09
Start: 16:30 PT
Duration: 47 minutes (recording stopped at 17:17)
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Samir (Redwood SE), Lena (TideBank Head of ML), Marco (Infra), Priya (Product)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
TideBank is evaluating tradeoffs between Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private. Primary drivers: predictable unit cost under heavy peak loads (payments time-sensitive), low-latency for fraud signal scoring, and strict data controls (KMS + VPC). They have a hard monthly budget for model inference and want clear per-token economics plus knobs (batching, KV cache, quant, routing).

Topics: budget cap, per-token pricing, batching/caching, fallback policies, dedicated capacity vs hosted, benchmark plan, security docs.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick intros?
[00:08] Lena (TideBank): Hi, Lena Cho, head of ML here. We're reworking real-time scoring for payments, trying to get latency under 120ms  tail for top-tier flows.
[00:15] Priya: Priya Desai, product, I'm on the procurement timeline and budget.
[00:18] Marco: Marco Alvarez, infra, happy to talk infra constraints and network.
[00:21] Maya: Great. Samir is our SE, he'll cover batching, cache, and the benchmark plan.
[00:27] Samir (Redwood SE): Hey, quick note — I might misuse some acronyms, apologies, and transcription may be off.
[00:35] Lena: No worries. Our ask: we need unit-econ predictability. We saw some numbers from other vendors where spikes blew past forecasted tokens. We want to know for common LLM flows — 64 to 512 token sequences — what's the expected per-token cost and where the savings come from. Also interested in fallback strategies if model capacity hits limits.
[01:12] Samir: Totally understood. High level: hosted is the fastest way to get started — predictable per-token pricing on average but variable under bursts unless you buy burst capacity. Dedicated gives you reserved GPUs so unit cost becomes more predictable at scale, and private (VPC/on-prem) gives max isolation but adds infra ops and some extra per-hour platform fee.
[01:41] Marco: For dedicated, what's the billing shape? Is it per-GPU hour + per-token, or flat? Our finance team hates surprises.
[01:49] Maya: Good question. Usually dedicated is a commitment model — monthly reserved pool priced by GPU/hour with a throughput expectation; token billing is folded into that or we present an effective per-token for your workload. We'll model both.
[02:05] Priya: So if we commit to a pool, can we get transparent token comparisons to hosted so we can justify spend?
[02:12] Maya: Yes, we'll send a spreadsheet showing hosted per-token, dedicated effective per-token at different utilization curves, and breakouts for batching/caching benefits.
[02:18] Lena: Walk us through the levers — batching, prefix/KV cache, and quantization — and their tradeoffs vs latency.
[02:28] Samir: Sure. Batching increases throughput and lowers per-token compute cost but adds queuing latency. For LOBs like TideBank with 100 qps peak for scoring, we often recommend micro-batching (short wait windows, e.g., 10-20ms) to avoid long tails. KV cache (we sometimes call it prefix cache) helps when many requests share context — big wins for chat-like or repeated prompts; for scoring it's less effective unless you have repeated user contexts. Quantization (4-bit/8-bit) reduces GPU memory and compute cost; for many open models we've validated quality-preserving quant profiles. But some finance-sensitive models may need higher precision — that impacts unit cost.
[03:25] Marco: On the KV cache, is the cache per-GPU? How much network traffic does cache invalidation cause if we run across region?
[03:33] Samir: Cache is local to the serving node, we maintain a distributed index for routing but invalidations are small messages. For private/VPC we can keep it on-site and avoid cross-region traffic. There are some mis-transcribed items in past notes where it reads K V cash — apologies.
[03:51] Lena: (laughs) noted. Ok — fallback behavior: we need a plan if our primary model hits capacity or fails. We can't have scoring fully degraded; maybe a cheaper/approx model returning a score with a confidence tag?
[04:07] Samir: Exactly. We support automated fallback chains: e.g., primary high-quality model -> lower-latency smaller model -> cached heuristic. Each stage has a defined quality/loss profile and we annotate responses. We can also route by policy: latency SLO first, or cost-priority.
[04:25] Priya: How do you model cost when fallbacks occur? It sounds like unit cost could spike if fallbacks are more expensive or if retries happen.
[04:33] Maya: We model expected token consumption per-request and probability mass of fallbacks under load. The spreadsheet will include scenario projections: normal, peak, and failure modes (e.g., 10% fallback rate).
[04:47] Marco: Are there hard limits we can set? Like reject beyond X tokens or degrade to local model only?
[04:52] Samir: Yes, you can set hard circuit-breakers and automatic quota-based rejections. Also tail-latency based routing — if the hosted pool is experiencing high tail, route to dedicated or smaller model.
[05:05] Lena: On privacy and KMS: we need end-to-end encryption and our own KMS. Does Redwood support customer-managed keys for private and dedicated?
[05:14] Maya: We do. Private supports customer KMS/HSM, and dedicated can be configured to use your KMS for key wrapping. Hosted supports envelope encryption with BYOK in some tiers; we'll send the security note.
[05:27] Marco: For networking, we need VPC peering and no outbound NAT for data plane egress — possible on private deployments?
[05:33] Samir: Yes, VPC/no-NAT is supported for private and dedicated in most regions. We'll include the network topology doc.
[05:42] Lena: Back to unit economics — can you show a worked example for a detection pipeline that does 100M tokens/month with 80% being short (<=64 tokens) and 20% long (256-512)?
[05:54] Samir: We'll put that in the spreadsheet. Quick verbal: batching helps most on short tokens because you can amortize kernel overhead; caching helps only if you have repeat contexts. Quant helps both by lowering per-token compute cost. Dedicated at 70-80% utilization typically yields the lowest cost per token. Hosted is simplest but requires burst allowances or you pay for burst.
[06:20] Priya: How do you recommend we think about forecasting — do you provide forecasts tied to SLOs?
[06:25] Maya: We provide per-route estimates by model, sequence length distribution, and desired latency SLOs. We'll show cost at 50th, 90th, and 99th percentile latency and effective token cost at those percentiles.
[06:38] Marco: Any tooling for seeing token-level breakdowns post-deploy? We need to reconcile our internal billing.
[06:44] Samir: Console provides token-level cost, route-level breakouts, and tracing. You can export line items for your billing system.
[06:50] Lena: Competitors sometimes bundle inference into opaque pricing. We need transparent math.
[06:55] Maya: That's our focus — we hand you the assumptions: model flops, effective tokens, batching window, quantization profile.
[07:03] (short cross-talk)
[07:10] Priya: Procurement note — we have a quarterly budget planning cycle; to hit next quarter we'll need initial pricing and an executive summary by two weeks.
[07:20] Maya: We'll prioritize delivering an exec summary and spreadsheets within three business days.
[07:25] Samir: For the benchmark, can you confirm expected QPS and any P95/P99 latency targets?
[07:31] Lena: We're targeting 50-120 qps in normal and spikes to 400 qps during peak, P95 under 120ms, P99 ideally under 220ms.
[07:42] Samir: Good specifics. We'll design a bench that sweeps sequence lengths and concurrency to simulate those peaks. We'll include both hosted and dedicated configs — note: hosted benchmark will rely on burst capacity settings.
[07:57] Marco: About burst: is it buyable as an add-on or auto-scaled? How do we avoid a surprise bill?
[08:04] Maya: For hosted we offer burst credits and quota alerts; you can cap burst so overages are blocked. For dedicated, you can configure autoscaling policies and set hard caps for cost control.
[08:16] Lena: What about caching strategy for scoring pipelines — we have many near-duplicate requests. Is prefix cache worth it?
[08:24] Samir: If you have repeat prompts or repeated user context, prefix cache shines. For near-duplicate requests you can use a similarity hash to hit the cache more often. We'll discuss tradeoffs in the plan.
[08:39] Priya: Any concerns about quantization causing misclassifications for fraud? We can't accept a hit in recall.
[08:46] Samir: We recommend running a quality A/B: quantized model vs baseline on a holdout set. Many models operate fine at 4-bit, but finance is conservative so 8-bit or selective quantization is common. We'll include regression thresholds in the eval plan.
[09:02] (background noise, somebody shuffling papers)
[09:10] Marco: On-device inference is not an option for us due to latency; private on-prem would be ok if ops can manage the GPU infrastructure. What's Redwood's support posture for private?
[09:20] Maya: We offer a private package with install playbooks, ops support add-on, and an optional managed services layer to reduce your burden. Costs are higher but you get full control.
[09:29] Lena: Timeline question: if we want pilot in Q1, what's a reasonable runway?
[09:34] Samir: Pilot could start within 4-6 weeks assuming we get env access and model artifacts. Benchmarks plus a two-week pilot run to gather production-like traffic.
[09:42] Priya: Procurement will need SOC 2 and penetration test attestations as part of vendor review.
[09:47] Maya: We'll share SOC 2 Type II report and recent pen test summary. Also KMS+network diagram.
[09:55] Lena: What's the typical fallback to smaller model cost delta? Example: big model costs X, small model cost Y — ballpark numbers?
[10:03] Samir: Rough ballpark: smaller model might be 30-60% cheaper per-token but quality drop depends on task. We'll quantify for your scoring model during the bench.
[10:14] Marco: Any auto-scaling lag concerns for sudden spikes? We need deterministic behavior for payments flows.
[10:20] Samir: We recommend reserved capacity for core flows and burst for tail. Autoscaling has warm-up windows; for deterministic behavior we prefer reserved/dedicated capacity.
[10:30] Priya: Will you include financial modeling for reserve-to-hosted transition? We want to know break-even utilization.
[10:37] Maya: Yes — typical break-even depends on utilization, model size, and quant. We'll compute a utilization curve in the spreadsheet.
[10:45] (transcription glitch, speaker labeled Speaker 2) Speaker 2: does Redwood support RBAC per-route?
[10:50] Samir: Yes, RBAC and token scoping so you can isolate prod vs dev routes.
[10:54] Lena: Ok, can we talk about SLA and incident response?
[10:58] Maya: Dedicated has SLA-backed latency and uptime targets. Hosted has standard uptime SLAs; private depends on the package. We have playbooks for incident triage and can set up alerting hooks to your pager.
[11:10] Priya: For the benchmark, can we include a chaos scenario where we force failover to fallback chain to see behavior under degraded conditions?
[11:17] Samir: Absolutely. We'll include a failure injection test to measure fallback rate, latency, and cost delta.
[11:24] Marco: Regarding observability retention — how long do you keep token traces? We have compliance needs for up to 90 days for auditing.
[11:31] Maya: Default retention is shorter but we offer extended retention as an add-on in enterprise plans; private gives you full control.
[11:38] (short pause)
[11:43] Lena: Anything we should watch out for in the spreadsheet assumptions? I'm worried about optimistic batching gains that don't materialize.
[11:50] Samir: Good point. We'll include conservative and optimistic assumptions for batch fill rates, and show sensitivity analysis: if batch fill is 50% vs 90% how unit costs change.
[11:59] Priya: On the commercial side — early commit discounts if we sign a 12-month reserved plan?
[12:04] Maya: Yes, there's tiered discounts for commits; we'll include modeled pricing for 6 and 12 month commitments.
[12:11] Marco: How do we instrument token counting to match your billing? We need to reconcile on day one.
[12:17] Samir: Console emits per-request token counts and there's an ingestable export you can import into your cost system. We'll provide ingestion docs.
[12:25] (background: someone on customer side typing)
[12:30] Lena: Ok let's set expectations: deliverables in the next 72 hours — spreadsheet, exec summary, SOC2 and network doc. Then schedule bench kickoff the following week if we accept.
[12:40] Maya: Confirmed. We'll target 72 hours for docs and propose bench dates.
[12:46] Priya: One more question — are there minimum commitments for dedicated?
[12:50] Maya: Typical entry is a 3-6 month reserved pool for small pilots; we'll include options.
[12:57] Samir: Also we'll note quant/regression tolerance thresholds so procurement and ML can sign off.
[13:05] (closing) Maya: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with action items. Any final questions?
[13:12] Lena: No, thanks.
[13:14] Priya: Thanks all.
[13:16] Marco: Thanks.
